headline: Sankaty Rip: First Bonito Flash, Bass Still Playing It by Dark
subhead: The first bonito showed on the south side this week — right on schedule — while stripers stay locked into low-light windows around Monomoy and the Shoals.
body_markdown:
Tuesday evening, working the Sankaty rip on the last of the ebb, I watched a school of something come up under a pod of bait and just erase it — no big splash, no birds working yet, just a boil that flattened out in about two seconds and left slick water where the bait had been. Too fast and too clean for bluefish. Too small a footprint for stripers. I made three casts with an epoxy jig before I even admitted to myself what I was hoping it was. Didn't connect that pass, but twenty minutes later a buddy running out of Monomoy texted me a photo of a bonito in the bottom of his boat, caught off the Vineyard side rips earlier that morning. First one I've had confirmed this year on our side of the Sound.

We said this was coming — flagged it a week back that the breachways and the Vineyard rips would see bonito within days, and here it is, right where we said it'd show first. It's not a push yet. It's scouts. One here, one there, working the edges where the current stacks bait against structure. Give it another week and I expect we'll start seeing them show consistently off Great Point and along the back side of Tuckernuck as water in the Sound proper catches up to what the open Atlantic side is already running. Right now the deep basin water is still a touch cool for a full-blown bonito show inside the Sound — the fish are hugging the warmer, current-scrubbed edges on the ocean side first. That's the pattern every year. Ocean rips first, Sound rips a week or two behind.

Stripers are still playing the summer game — tight to low light. Anything you catch during the heat of the day around here right now, you're catching almost by accident. The real window is that hour before full light and the hour after sunset, and Monomoy has been the most consistent piece of water for it. With the wind out of the southwest most mornings, the rips off the elbow and down toward the Powder Hole have been setting up clean — current pushing against the wind builds a nice standing wave and stacks bait right against the bar. I've had the best luck working a 2-ounce white or olive Deceiver on an intermediate line, swinging it through the seam where the white water meets the green, letting it sink on the drop before starting the strip. Fish have been mostly schoolies with the occasional 28- to 32-incher mixed in, nothing to write home about size-wise, but steady enough that two or three fish in that dawn window feels normal right now.

Chatham inlet and the back side of the Powder Hole have been doing similar work on the outgoing, especially with bunker starting to filter through — where you find the pods of bunker getting nervous, that's where the bigger fish are sitting, and that's also where the bluefish have been thickest. Cocktail blues, mostly two to four pounds, but a few chunkier ones mixed in chewing through wire leader like it's nothing. If you're throwing bucktails for bass and keep getting bit off, that's your answer — the blues have moved into the same bait as the stripers and they're not shy about it. Small wire leader or a heavier fluorocarbon bite tippet has saved me more lures than I'd like to admit this week.

Fluke have been the one truly dependable bite regardless of hour, and the full-moon tide swing this week sharpened it up nicely. Horseshoe Shoal edges and the deeper cuts off Monomoy Point have both been holding fish — nothing enormous, mostly 16 to 19 inches with a scattered keeper over 20, but good numbers on the drift with white Gulp Swimming Mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, working the drop-offs where the sandy flats fall into 15 to 25 feet. The stronger current from the full moon has kept the bite compressed right around the tide changes — dead slack and you might as well be anchored for lunch, but the hour on either side of the change has been lighting up nicely with fish stacked on the current edges.

Albies are still a no-show around here, and I wouldn't expect them yet. Great Point usually doesn't see its first real wave until closer to the end of August into early September, once the bait gets pushed hard against the rip on the ebb and the water out at the tip cools a shade from the deeper Nantucket Shoals current mixing in. I'll be out there checking every few days regardless — that first blitz off the Point, with the terns wheeling and the surface exploding all along the rip, is the moment I wait for all summer, and I'll know it the second I see it.

For the coming week, I'd focus mornings on Monomoy for stripers before the sun gets up, keep an eye on the Sankaty and Great Point rips for any more bonito flashes on calm mornings, and lean on the fluke drift over Horseshoe Shoal around the tide changes if the bass window comes up empty. The southwest wind pattern looks like it'll hold, which keeps those Monomoy rips working in our favor — just watch the afternoon sea breeze building stronger by midweek if you're running a small boat out toward the Shoals.
